utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-R77.2-I, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Seselj, are you receiving a translation in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I'm not receiving any interpretation. I haven't got any translation. Your words were not interpreted to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I will repeat them, in the expectation that it is now occurring, and the Court Officer will check that you're switched on to the correct channel to receive the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm on the right channel now and have heard the interpretation of what you said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Splendid. Now, appearances. Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. My name --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. MacFarlane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: My name is Bruce MacFarlane. I'm an attorney from Canada. I appear as amicus curiae Prosecutor, and with me this afternoon and for the course of the trial is Lori Ann Wanlin, also from Canada.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I see and I understand, Mr. Seselj, that you are intending today to represent yourself.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully intend to represent myself, and not only today, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'll come back to that in a little while, Mr. Seselj. I think, probably, as you are representing yourself, I should, as a matter of precaution, although I'm sure you've become well familiar with the matter already, remind you in particular that under the Statute and the Rules of Evidence and Procedure, you enjoy the right to remain silent at any time during the proceedings. Are you not obliged to say anything. That is a matter for your decision. There are, of course, as I'm sure you have become well aware, other rights to which you are entitled under the Statute and the Rules. Just so that you know of them again, in particular in Articles 20 and 21 of the Statute you'll find an identification of significant rights of an accused, and the Rules of the Tribunal deal in many ways with aspects of the procedure that will be followed. I know, from what little I know of your own legal training and background, and your time here, that you are quite familiar with those matters, but as a matter of precaution, I just draw them again to your attention. It should be mentioned that on the 21st of January this year, acting under Rule 77(C), an order in lieu of an indictment was issued against Mr. Seselj. I will refer to this as "the indictment." An order was also made for amicus curiae to be appointed to prosecute the indictment, and it was on the 11th of February that the acting Registrar appointed Mr. Bruce MacFarlane, QC, as amicus curiae in this case. Now, at this stage, by way of summary, Mr. Seselj, I would simply remind you that you are charged with one count of contempt of the Tribunal, which is punishable under Rule 77(A) of the Rules, for knowingly and willfully interfering with the administration of justice by disclosing confidential information in violation of orders granting protective measures and by disclosing excerpts of the written statement of a witness in a book published in or about November of 2007. As you've been in the custody of the Tribunal now for quite some time, I don't think there's any need, as we would do if this was your very first appearance here, to go through the formalities of confirming your identity and personal details. I think we can take it that they are all well known. I would, though, as a matter of precaution, just inquire whether you accept that you are the Vojislav Seselj named in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, not only am I the man, but I'm very proud of being that particular person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I thought you might well accept that you are the person charged, Mr. Seselj, so we won't go further in going through all the formalities of your identity. Now, I understand, Mr. Seselj, that you have received the indictment in your own language. Can I be sure that's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct, but I'd like to draw your attention to the fact that I have received two versions of that same order which today we're going to refer to as "indictment." There is a public and a confidential version, and I think that today, in the courtroom, we should have the confidential version read out and to abolish any confidentiality over that version, because it protects the identity of the protected witnesses; however, mention is made therein of the name of the book in which I allegedly published their identity. And in the public indictment, the title of the book is not mentioned. We have a well-known name in the title of this book, and the title is very exotic. However, that individual is not a protected witness in any of the trials appearing before this Tribunal, in any of the proceedings, and I think that since I am being tried for this book, the public ought to know the exact title of the book. There's no reason why that should be held back and secret, and if somebody doesn't like being mentioned in the title of the book, then they can address the amicus curiae Prosecutor in this case and take it up with him. But I think that you can only try me on the basis of a public indictment and not a secret, confidential indictment, and that is why I demand that we read out that confidential indictment, and any mention of the book and the book's title be uttered in open session, because what happened in another proceedings against me, when I mentioned the title of the book, the Trial Chamber decides to redact the transcript and decides to move into private session. And I think that is quite impermissible in these proceedings, because in these proceedings we are duty-bound only to protect the names of the protected witnesses from the main trial or, rather, any proceedings held in this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I rather take it, from what you've been saying, that you will be able to assure me that you've read the indictment and understood its contents, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Judge, and I'm in a position to plead today, without having to waste a month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a splendid position, Mr. Seselj. You realise that I need to take some of these steps to ensure that you are not proceeding in ignorance of your rights and position, particularly because you're not represented. Now, I'm afraid there is in place an order attaching confidentiality to certain elements of the indictment. I am not in a position to vary that order. Therefore, if you want the indictment read in the full form, you being aware there is a full form which identifies individuals and a book, and there is a form when those details are omitted, if you want it in the full form, it will need to be read in closed/private session. Otherwise, we can read it simply omitting the identification of witnesses and of the book, and we can do it in public session. Which would you prefer today, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I'm absolutely opposed to any type of closed or private session, and I demand that these proceedings be held in completely open session. So you can read out the portions that you think can be read out in open session, and if you have been appointed the Pre-Trial Judge, then you will have to deal with this question of confidentiality very soon, because there's no sense in the indictment remaining confidential. I'm being tried here, and the public doesn't know why I'm being tried. The public must be made aware of what I'm being tried for. Even had I killed a man, the name of the person who I killed would have to be stated in open session, publicly, and not for the fact that I spoke against some protagonist, the person who was a protagonist of American policy and CIA policy in Belgrade. I don't see the reason for the identity of this person to be hidden from the public. Now, perhaps the problem is that the decision was made in a confidential form, but from the initial appearance this question must be tried by the Trial Chamber acting in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Seselj. The reason for the confidentiality is that there is a trial ongoing involving you in which witnesses and other material is of concern. For that reason, the confidentiality order has been made. Whether it can be varied or removed entirely at some stage in these proceedings is a matter that will have to be addressed in due course by the Trial Chamber when that is appointed and whoever it may be. What I propose to do, therefore, Mr. Seselj, is to -- I think it better probably if I read the indictment, rather than the Court Officer, because with a bit of luck I can be careful not to mention those parts which are confidential. If I could remind you that the order in lieu of an indictment says that you, born in 1954 in Sarajevo, in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and currently on trial before the Tribunal, is charged with one count of contempt of the Tribunal, pursuant to Rule 77(A)(ii) of the Rules as detailed below. Then follow three paragraphs of factual allegations: 1. In its decision of 13 March 2003, 1 June 2005, 6 July 2005, and 8 November 2006, the Trial Chamber trying the case of Prosecutor against Vojislav Seselj ordered various protective measures in respect of three witnesses identified in the indictment by pseudonyms. In its decision on adopting protective measures of the 30th of August, 2007, the Seselj Trial Chamber ordered that the use of pseudonyms, as well as image and face distortion, remain applicable in respect of these three witnesses. The Trial Chamber also prohibited the disclosure of the names, addresses, places of residence, or any other information which may identify the protected witnesses, and from this disclosing this information to any third party, except when this information is directly and specifically necessary for the preparation and presentation of the Defence case. In addition, the disclosure of the written statement of a witness, identified by pseudonym, was prohibited by the Trial Chamber's decision on Prosecution's motion for order of non-disclosure filed on 13 March 2003. The second paragraph: In or about November 2007, a book which is named, authored by you, was published. The book contains numerous references to the three witnesses, including their real names, occupations, places of residence, which enable the identification of these witnesses. The book also contains excerpts of the written statement of one of the protected witnesses. The third paragraph: At the time of the publication of the book, you had knowledge of the order prohibiting the disclosure of the written statement of that identified witness and of the orders adopting protective measures in respect of and ordered specifically prohibiting the disclosure of information which may identify the three protected witnesses. Then follows the charge. By your acts and omissions, you committed contempt of the Tribunal, punishable under this Tribunal's inherent power, and Rule 77(A)(ii) of the Rules, for knowingly and willfully interfering with the administration of justice by disclosing confidential information in violation of orders granting protective measures and by disclosing excerpts of the written statements of the identified witness in the book, which book was published in or about November 2007. Now, I've read there with those variations only so as not to disclose the pseudonyms and the name of the book, and that is the indictment which is brought against you under this order in lieu of an indictment. You've indicated that you wish to plead today. I welcome that, Mr. Seselj. I should remind you, though, that you may, if you wish, defer that for up to 30 days, but if it is your wish to plead, do you plead guilty or not guilty to that indictment, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to enter a plea straight away, and it is: Not guilty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Seselj, and for your preparedness to move in such a timely fashion. I hope it will be possible to maintain the speed so that this matter can be dealt with as promptly as possible. I will ensure that the Registrar records that you have entered a plea of not guilty in respect of the indictment. Now, I need to return, Mr. Seselj, to the issue of legal representation. You've indicated quite clearly that you have chosen not [sic] to represent yourself. As a matter of caution and to try and ensure that your decision is fully and properly informed, I would simply like to point out to you that the principal advantages of having legal representation is that you would have skilled and experienced advice and assistance as to your own legal position in this matter and in the conduct of your case, if you were to decide to be represented rather than to represent yourself; and of course it would be open to you to make application for assistance with respect to the cost of legal representation to the Registrar. I remind you of those matters so that you may take them into account, and if you wish to change your view and have legal representation, you are, of course, free to do that at any stage of what should follow in these proceedings. Also as a precaution, Mr. Seselj, I know I probably don't need to say any of these things, but so that it's clear, I want to remind you of the provisions of Rule 63. That Rule lays out the conditions on which the Prosecutor may interview you even after this initial appearance. Now, in this case, you should read the Rule referring to the Prosecutor clearly as referring to the amicus curiae who's been appointed, Mr. MacFarlane; and under that Rule any questioning of you by the Prosecutor, or people on his behalf, should not proceed without the presence of counsel representing you unless you voluntarily and expressly agree that the interview can proceed without your counsel present. If you do commence without counsel, should there be some interview attempted, you may at any time make it clear that you do not wish to proceed further until counsel are present. Now, I've just tried there to remind you of an essential attribute of Rule 63 so that you are reminded of its content, and you'll also see in that Rule that anything that you say will be audio- and video-recorded, and you will be cautioned at the beginning should there be any occasion on which the Prosecutor seeks to interview you or have you interviewed. That may not occur at all, don't think it must occur, but if it does occur, I want to be sure that you're aware of your position. The next matter I would just mention in passing is Rule 66. That concerns the materials that supported the order in lieu of indictment. I see, from a filing by the amicus curiae that I have just received, and which no doubt is now in the process of being translated for you, that the amicus curiae is well aware of the disclosure obligations of the Rules. I won't deal any further with the matter of disclosure at this stage. If it is necessary, a decision will issue in due course dealing with matters raised in the motion. But you will be aware of those proceedings as they continue, Mr. Seselj, and of course you may make submissions in writing, as you think appropriate, as they continue. The Trial Chamber will, in due course, as soon as disclosure is resolved, and any other procedural steps, be making orders as to status in pre-trial conferences, if they are necessary and, hopefully in the not-distant future, an order as to the commencement date for trial, so I look forward to those possibilities arising. Now, I've tried to deal, this afternoon, with the matters that I think are important that you be reminded of, Mr. Seselj, so that your essential rights are brought again to your knowledge and so that you can be alert as matters proceed as to what those rights are; and I have, myself, looked at the proceedings so far with a view to ensuring that the requirements have been satisfied this far. Is there any other matter which, first of all, you, Mr. MacFarlane, consider needs to be raised today?

utterances.speaker: MR. MACFARLANE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Not at this point. I anticipate that there might be other matters, but I don't have anything to raise at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it's essentially a first hearing for Mr. Seselj. He's cooperated in moving the matter along quickly with the plea of not guilty, so that hopefully we can get to the other pre-trial procedural matters quickly. Now, Mr. Seselj, is there any matter concerning this initial appearance that you feel needs to be raised today?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly. Probably there was a mistake in the interpretation at the beginning of what you started to say this afternoon, because the interpreter said that I would not be representing myself. I think that's a mistake, and you said that I had decided to represent myself. So I'm saying that for the public, to make that quite clear, not to leave the wrong impression. The second point is this: As far as talking to the Prosecutor is concerned, of course the Prosecutor has the right to issue an order for the guards to bring me in for an interview, but it depends on me, whether I'll talk to him or not. And I consider that I have nothing to discuss with the Prosecutor. He has the indictment before him, I have set the outlines of my Defence case, and anything we need to do can be done in the courtroom here. So I have no reason to discuss any matters with the Prosecutor. If they force me to go there, I'll sit there silently and stay there for as long as it takes. Now, with respect to disclosure, as far as I remember, the Rule says that the Prosecutor is duty-bound, within the space of one month, to provide me with all the documents attending the indictment. And the fourth point I wish to make is this: Because I'm representing myself, Judge, I require that I be allowed to sit in the first row so that I can be in the courtroom visually and on a par in the courtroom with the opposite side, that is to say, the Prosecutor, as of the next proceedings, whether it be a status conference, or a pre-trial conference, or whatever the proceedings accord.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You started your comments by saying that you'd be brief. You have observed your own requirement. That's a matter that I am appreciative of, Mr. Seselj. What you have said discloses that you correctly understand your position and your entitlements. There is nothing I need to add to those matters. As to where you sit in the courtroom is a matter according to the ordinary practice of this Tribunal, and subject to any order that might be made as the matter progresses, the ordinary procedures of the Tribunal will apply. I would like to thank counsel for their attendance and assistance today. The matters that need to be dealt with on an initial appearance have been concluded, and I will now adjourn.
